finding: Comparison figures are not like-for-like (6 knots, power 1.5 against the chosen 12 knots, power 2). The README (lines 202-203) and A35 (AUDIT_LOG.md line 931) set the chosen model's held-out 5.0% / 18.9% beside 'without interactions 7.2% / 28.8%' and 'with the strongest 20 numeric pairs 5.5% / 19.6%'. Both comparison rows were fitted at 6 knots and power 1.5. A35 does not say so at all, and the README gives '(6 knots)' only for the no-interaction case. A reader therefore takes 20 pairs to be worse than the chosen 10, when at equal knots and power 20 pairs is better than 10. The interaction gain is also overstated, because part of the 7.2% to 5.0% fall comes from going from 6 to 12 knots.
evidence: ev_a35_surrogate_specification.csv, held out. 10 pairs, 6 knots, power 1.5: MSLE 0.009804, median 0.057341, p95 0.200979. 20 pairs, 6 knots, power 1.5: 0.009135, 0.055365, 0.195726. 0 pairs, 6 knots, power 1.5: 0.017150, 0.072008, 0.287897. Chosen (10 pairs, 12 knots, power 2): 0.008431, 0.050098, 0.189475. Suggested fix: Quote the like-for-like baseline: at 6 knots and power 1.5, no interactions gives 7.2% / 28.8%, 10 pairs 5.7% / 20.1% and 20 pairs 5.5% / 19.6%. Say this in both the README and A35.
verifier: Reproduced from ev_a35_surrogate_specification.csv. The comparison rows are (0, 6, 1.5) with MSLE 0.017150, median 0.072008, p95 0.287897, and (20, 6, 1.5) with 0.009135, 0.055365, 0.195726. The like-for-like 10-pair row (10, 6, 1.5) is 0.009804, 0.057341, 0.200979; the chosen (10, 12, 2) is 0.008431, 0.050098, 0.189475. A reader comparing 20 pairs (5.5% / 19.6%) with the chosen 5.0% / 18.9% would conclude 20 pairs is worse, but at equal settings 20 pairs beats 10. The interaction benefit is also overstated: like-for-like it is 7.2% to 5.7%, not 7.2% to 5.0%. Medium is fair.

finding: 'Each of the 26 numerics is a cubic spline with 12 knots' is wrong for 13 of the 25 splines. FactorSpec drops duplicate quantile knots (np.unique), so 12 knots is only the number requested. evidence: Pieces per term in buildings_surrogate_spline_pieces.csv, minus 1, give the distinct knots. Recomputing np.unique(np.quantile(x, linspace(0,1,12))) on rows_inputs_buildings.parquet gives the same counts: 11 for days_quote_to_inception and years_at_address; 5 for household_size, bedrooms and x_clay_dry; 4 for voluntary_excess, renewal_count, customer_since_year and flood_zone; 3 for discount_applied, prior_claims_5y, licence_points and x_fz3_rain. A parameter recount (1 + 304 categorical + 1 band + 234 basis + 5 missing = 545) matches the 545 reported. Suggested fix: Write 'a cubic spline with up to 12 knots at quantiles (fewer where quantiles coincide: 3 to 11 for 13 of them); missed_payments_12m, with only 2 distinct knots, is banded'.
verifier: Confirmed two ways. Pieces per term in buildings_surrogate_spline_pieces.csv, minus 1, give 12 distinct knots for 12 terms and 3 to 11 for 13 terms. finding: Flood-zone relativities overstate the trees' effect by 23% (zone 4) and 67% (zone 5). The README offers the surrogate 'for showing buildings small claims as rating relativities', but its flood-zone effect does not match the trees' conditional effect. Zone totals on the 2025 rows are fine. The trouble is that the zone effect is confounded with elevation and distance to river, and the cross that should hold that interaction bands flood zone as <=1, 2, >=3 (S2). So zone 5 is loaded far more heavily than the trees load it, and an atypical quote in zone 4 or 5 is overpriced.
evidence: Moved every 2025 row to one flood zone, with x_fz3_rain rebuilt by the export's own formula (a rebuild of the data reproduces the column exactly), and scored the trees with export_excel.score_trees (matches small_claim within 7.3e-6) against the refitted surrogate (matches the export within 1.3e-15, factor 1.0007452516611526). Trees x1.362 / surrogate x1.681 in zone 4 (+23.4%); trees x1.726 / surrogate x2.889 in zone 5 (+67.4%). Zones 1-3 are within +0.3% to -2.0%. On the rows really in each zone, in sample: zone 4 -1.2%, zone 5 +0.1%. With the interaction bands at the trees' thresholds (S2), the zone 4 and zone 5 gaps shrink to +8.0% and +23.9%. Suggested fix: Do not present the flood-zone (or any interacted) term as a stand-alone relativity, or band the crosses at the trees' thresholds (S2). Before calling a relativity the model's, check it against the trees' partial dependence.
verifier: I reproduced this exactly with a scratch script that imports the runner's functions. Refitted surrogate vs exported rows: 0.0 difference (factor 1.0007452516611526). score_trees (double precision) vs small_claim: max 7.28e-6. The x_fz3_rain rebuild matches the column exactly. With every row moved to one zone, surrogate/trees totals are: zone 1 +0.3%, zone 2 +0.2%, zone 3 -2.0%, zone 4 +23.4%, zone 5 +67.4%. Against the actual book, the trees give x1.362 and x1.681 for zone 4 and x1.726 and x2.889 for zone 5. Rows really in each zone, in sample: zone 4 -1.2%, zone 5 +0.1%. Refitted with tree-threshold bands: +8.0% and +23.9%. The bias also shows on real 2025 rows. Zone-4 rows at elevation 3-5.9 m (386 rows) are +18.0% and at 5.9-9.5 m (35 rows) +31.1%. Zone-5 rows at 3-5.9 m (10 rows) are +67.3%. The low-elevation rows that dominate these zones are -3.5% and -0.1%, which is why the zone totals look fine. This is not only a counterfactual effect. Severity: high holds for the README's offered use 'showing buildings small claims as rating relativities' and for atypical zone 4/5 risks; pricing the 2025 book by zone total is not affected.

finding: Quintile interaction bands collapse and miss the trees' split points; tree-threshold bands cut held-out MSLE by 39%. interaction_bands uses marginal quintiles. On skewed or discrete features these collapse, so the 'five-band' crosses (README line 181, A35) have 3 bands for flood_zone, prior_claims_5y and x_clay_dry and 2 for x_fz3_rain. The flood bands (<=1, (1,2], >2) pool zones 3-5, but almost all of the trees' flood-zone gain sits at their zone-4 and zone-5 splits. Errors cluster in exactly those cells. Banding at the trees' own thresholds is better, simpler and uses fewer parameters.
evidence: From the shipped terms file: flood_zone band uppers 1, 2, inf; x_fz3_rain 0, inf. From buildings_xgboost.json: flood-zone split gain is 91.8% at threshold 4 and 7.7% at 5. Experiment (same seed-1 80/20 split, 10 pairs, 12 knots, p=2, runner functions only): interaction bands at each feature's 4 highest-gain tree thresholds give 489 parameters against 545. Held-out MSLE 0.00511 against 0.00843 (-39%), median 4.4% against 5.0%, p95 14.6% against 18.9%, p99 21.2% against 31.5%, largest 61% against 103%. On a policy split (seed 2): 0.00516 against 0.00830. Flood zone banded by value only: 0.00763. Where the shipped fit goes wrong, from 20-quantile segments: flood-zone-4 rows have MSLE 0.034 against 0.0084 overall, and 10.6% of them are in the worst 1%; zone 5 has MSLE 0.030. The worst segment total is the 15th-20th percentile of elevation, at +6.3% (5.5% of cost). The trees put 64% of their elevation gain at thresholds between the 13th and 16th percentiles, between the 9.1% and 18.2% knots. Suggested fix: Build the interaction bands, and preferably the knots or bands of the main effects, at the trees' highest-gain thresholds, not at marginal quantiles. Correct 'five-band' in the README and A35.
verifier: Reproduced. The exported interaction bands are: flood_zone uppers 1, 2, inf; prior_claims_5y 0, 1, inf; x_clay_dry 0, 0.569, inf; x_fz3_rain 0, inf. So 'five-band' in README line 181, A35 (AUDIT_LOG line 925) and the runner docstring is wrong for 4 of the 8 features. From buildings_xgboost.json, flood-zone split gain is 91.8% at threshold 4 and 7.7% at 5. On the same seed-1 80/20 split (10 pairs, 12 knots, p=2), bands at each feature's 4 highest-gain tree thresholds give 489 parameters against 545. Held-out: MSLE 0.00511 against 0.00843, median 4.37% against 5.01%, p95 14.6% against 18.9%, p99 21.2% against 31.5%, largest 61% against 103%. Flood zone banded by value alone: 0.00763. In sample, MSLE is 0.0336 for zone 4 and 0.0306 for zone 5, against 0.00835 overall. 10.5% of zone-4 rows are in the worst 1% (the finding says 10.6%; the difference is the tie rule). The 15-20th percentile elevation segment is +6.4% on 5.4% of cost. Tree thresholds 2.1, 2.2 and 2.5 m sit at the 13.0th, 14.6th and 16.1st percentiles, hold 64.3% of the elevation gain, and fall between the 1.5 m and 2.7 m knots. finding: Comparison figures are confounded: 20 pairs looks worse than 10 but is better at equal settings. The README and A35 set the 20-pair and no-interaction results (both fitted at 6 knots, p=1.5) beside the chosen 10-pair, 12-knot, p=2 headline. A reader concludes that more interactions hurt (5.5% against 5.0%). At equal settings, 20 pairs beats 10. A35 line 931 does not state the knots at all.
evidence: ev_a35_surrogate_specification.csv at 6 knots, p=1.5. 10 pairs: MSLE 0.009804, median 5.73%, p95 20.10%. 20 pairs: 0.009135, 5.54%, 19.57%. 0 pairs: 0.017150, 7.20%, 28.79%. Chosen (12 knots, p=2): 0.008431, 5.01%, 18.95%. Suggested fix: Compare against the 10-pair fit at 6 knots, p=1.5 (5.7% / 20.1%), or fit the comparisons at the chosen 12 knots, p=2. State the settings in A35 too.
verifier: Checked against ev_a35_surrogate_specification.csv. At 6 knots, p=1.5: 10 pairs MSLE 0.009804, median 5.73%, p95 20.10%; 20 pairs 0.009135, 5.54%, 19.57%; 0 pairs 0.017150, 7.20%, 28.79%. The chosen fit (12 knots, p=2) is 0.008431, 5.01%, 18.95%. README line 202 gives '(6 knots)' only for the no-interaction case and never gives the power. AUDIT_LOG line 931 gives no settings at all. finding: Sum insured at or above the 2025 maximum is priced about 17% below the trees. The sum-insured spline peaks near the 99.1st percentile and then falls to the 2025 maximum. The constant extrapolation holds that lower value beyond the maximum, while the trees are flat there. So the largest houses, and every quote at or above the 2025 maximum, get a lower relativity than a house at the 99th percentile. That is non-monotone and contrary to the trees. The README's usage notes give no warning about inputs outside the 2025 range.
evidence: Spline pieces evaluated with export_excel.eval_pieces: log contribution 0.392 at p99, 0.346 at p99.9, 0.194 at the maximum, peak 0.393 at percentile 0.991; the last cubic piece runs from percentile 0.909. Top-decile-SI rows moved to SI = p99: surrogate/trees total +1.1%; to p99.9: -3.5%; to the maximum or twice it: -17.0%. All rows at the maximum: -17.1%. In sample, the 53 rows at or above p99.9 are at -5.0%. Other edges with all rows moved: elevation at its 2025 minimum +7.3%, at 1.5 x its maximum +6.8%; x_clay_dry at its maximum +10.6%. Suggested fix: Put the boundary knots at interior quantiles (for example the 1st and 99th) with constant extrapolation, or band the extreme tail, or constrain the top piece. In the README, say that inputs beyond the 2025 range need the trees.
verifier: Reproduced with eval_pieces on the exported pieces. Sum-insured log contribution is 0.392 at p99, 0.346 at p99.9 and 0.194 at the maximum, with a peak of 0.393 at the 99.1st percentile. The last cubic piece starts at the 90.9th percentile, and its upper knot is the 2025 maximum. Moving the top-decile rows to p99 gives +1.1%, to p99.9 -3.5%, and to the max or twice the max -17.0%. All rows at the max: -17.1%. The 53 rows at or above p99.9, in sample: -5.0%. The trees are flat there: their largest sum-insured threshold, about 439,000, sits at the 95.4th percentile, and they give identical predictions at the max and at twice the max. Other edges: elevation at its minimum +7.3%, at 1.5x its maximum +6.8%; x_clay_dry at its maximum +10.6%. The surrogate section has no warning about inputs outside the 2025 range. Medium is fair: the 2025 book is barely affected; relativities and quotes are.

finding: Missing numeric inputs in quotes deviate strongly from the trees; the surrogate's note says 'developed fit'. 20 of the 25 splines saw no missing values in 2025. For those, a missing value contributes 0, an arbitrary point on the curve, and the interaction falls to OTHER or the base level. The trees instead send a missing value down each split's learned default branch. The exported note still reads 'no missing values in the developed fit', which is wrong for a fit on 2025 rows: fitted_on was threaded only into the categorical note. The surrogate's README section does not warn about this.
evidence: buildings_surrogate_terms.csv: 20 'spline missing' rows carry the 'developed fit' note. Whole book with one input set missing, surrogate/trees total: sum_insured -29.3%, elevation_m +22.3%, prior_claims_5y -17.9%, year_built +11.2%, voluntary_excess +6.7%. distance_to_river_km, which has 2025 missing rows, is -0.2%. Suggested fix: Use the fitted_on text in the spline-missing note. In the surrogate section, say that a quote with a missing numeric that the 2025 rows never lack must be rejected or priced with the trees.
verifier: Partly real, overstated; severity should be low. Confirmed: 20 'spline missing' rows in buildings_surrogate_terms.csv carry 'no missing values in the developed fit', which is wrong for a fit on 2025 rows, because fitted_on reaches only the categorical note (export_excel.py line 192). The whole-book deviations reproduce exactly: sum_insured -29.3%, elevation +22.3%, prior claims -17.9%, year built +11.2%, voluntary excess +6.7%, distance to river -0.2%. The framing that the trees follow a 'learned default branch' does not hold. In the developed training data, sum_insured and voluntary_excess (policies_buildings), elevation_m and year_built (addresses) and prior_claims_5y (customers) have 0 missing values. Every tree split on those five features sends a missing value right (0% left), which is XGBoost's fixed default, not a learned direction. A missing value there is undefined in both models, so 'price it with the trees' is not a fix; rejecting the quote is, and that applies to the trees too. The five features that are missing in 2025 do get fitted missing indicators.

finding: 60 of 545 columns are exactly aliased, so the term tables are not identifiable relativities. Two things alias columns: splines on variables with only a few values carry as many columns as the variable has values, or more, and the crosses contain their features' main effects. Only the L2 penalty settles how the effect is shared between terms. Predictions are fine, but a single term can mislead. '545 parameters' overstates the identifiable count.
evidence: SVD of the final design matrix: 545 columns, numerical rank 485 (tolerance 1e-9). Distinct values against spline columns: voluntary_excess 4/5, discount_applied 3/4, licence_points 4/4, flood_zone 5/5, bedrooms 7/6, household_size 7/6. The null directions also involve the prior_claims_5y*x_clay_dry cells with soil_type. Flood-zone spline relative to zone 1: zone 2 at -0.305 log (x0.74). Adding its interaction terms, the book-average centred contributions are zone 1 -0.205 and zone 2 -0.219, so roughly level. The spline split is stable across alpha 1e-5 to 1e-3 (-0.303 to -0.290), so the aliasing is resolved by the minimum-norm split, not by the data. Suggested fix: Band or treat as categorical the numerics with few values. Present the relativity of any interacted feature as its combined effect, the spline plus its crosses, never the spline alone. Report the identifiable parameter count.
verifier: Reproduced. The final design matrix plus intercept has 545 columns and numerical rank 485 (matrix_rank, and at relative tolerances 1e-12 to 1e-6), so 60 columns are aliased. Distinct values against spline columns: voluntary_excess 4/5, discount_applied 3/4, licence_points 4/4, flood_zone 5/5. One small error: bedrooms and household_size, at 7 values and 6 columns, are saturated, not aliased. The flood_zone spline alone puts zone 2 at -0.305 log against zone 1. Adding the flood crosses, averaged over the book, gives -0.223 and -0.226 in my run (the finding's -0.205 and -0.219 average differently). Either way the two zones are level, as the trees are (zone 2/zone 1 = 1.001). The spline's zone 2 minus zone 1 is -0.303 at alpha 1e-5 and -0.290 at 1e-3, so the penalty, not the data, settles the split. Reading a spline term alone as a relativity misleads.

finding: Power 2 against 1.5 is within split noise, and a cost-weighted criterion prefers 1 or 1.5. Exposure-weighted MSLE is a sensible criterion and robust to dropping the weights, but the 0.1% gap between p=2 and p=1.5 is far smaller than the 4% seed-to-seed range of the held-out estimate. Errors concentrate in the highest-rate risks, so a premium-weighted view matters for pricing, and on that view p=2 is the worst of the three powers at 12 knots.
evidence: Seed-1 split, 12 knots. MSLE exposure-weighted: p2 0.00843, p1.5 0.00844. Unweighted: 0.00850 for both. Cost-weighted: p1 0.01093, p1.5 0.01119, p2 0.01201. Chosen spec across seeds and split types: MSLE 0.00830 to 0.00865. The top decile of the trees' rate holds 31% of cost, with in-sample p95 error 29%; the top decile of the surrogate's rate has p95 34%. Suggested fix: State that the power choice is a tie, or choose on a cost-weighted measure, or on several seeds or folds.
verifier: The numbers reproduce. Seed 1, 12 knots: exposure-weighted MSLE p1.5 0.00844, p2 0.00843; unweighted 0.00850 for both; cost-weighted p1 0.01093, p1.5 0.01119, p2 0.01201. The chosen spec on five row splits and five policy splits ranges 0.00832 to 0.00873. The top decile of the trees' rate holds 30.9% of cost with p95 error 29.3%; the top decile of the surrogate's rate has p95 34.1%. But the tie is already disclosed: README lines 189-190 say powers 2 and 1.5 'are practically level (0.00843 against 0.00844)', and A35 says the same. The README states and reasons the criterion (gamma 'weighs every policy's relative error alike'). Preferring a cost-weighted criterion is a modelling preference, not a defect.

finding: Knot cap is at the grid edge; knot placement, not count, is the binding constraint. The stated 'lowest held-out wins' rule would pick 20 knots, and the cap is a disclosed judgement. That judgement is defensible on diminishing returns: MSLE falls 3.3% at 16 knots and 4.2% at 20. Banding at the trees' thresholds (S2) gains ten times as much. The grid was also extended after seeing a boundary win, with selection on the same 20%. The cross-fit below shows no material optimism from that.
evidence: Evidence file: MSLE 0.008431 at 12 knots, 0.008157 at 16, 0.008081 at 20. Five-fold policy-grouped out-of-fold scores on every row, chosen spec: MSLE 0.00852, median 5.07%, p95 18.8%, p99 31.8%, largest 115%, total -0.07%. Suggested fix: Keep the cap but give the reason as placement: put knots at the trees' thresholds.
verifier: Not a defect, and the finding says so itself. The 'lowest held-out wins' rule in the README applies to the 15 stated candidates (4 to 12 knots); 16 and 20 knots are labelled comparison only, and the cap is stated with its reason. The figures check out: MSLE 0.008431, 0.008157 and 0.008081 (-3.3% and -4.2%); median 5.01%, 4.95% and 4.90%. A35 discloses that the grid was extended after 8 knots won. My 5-fold policy-grouped cross-fit of the chosen spec (MSLE 0.0085, median 5.07%, p95 18.8%, p99 31.7%, total -0.07%) shows no optimism from selecting on the same 20%. The proposed fix only rewords the rationale.

finding: 'Intercept multiplied by 1.00075' is literally wrong. The log-scale intercept was raised by ln(1.00075), so the prediction is multiplied by 1.00075, not the intercept. The exported intercept already includes the change, but a builder who follows the text could apply it a second time, to the log intercept.
evidence: surrogate_buildings.py line 202: intercept_ + np.log(factor). The reconciliation file gives factor 1.0007452516611526. Suggested fix: Say 'the intercept was raised by ln(1.00075) (predictions x1.00075); the exported intercept already includes it'.
verifier: Confirmed. surrogate_buildings.py line 202 adds np.log(factor) to the log-scale intercept, and the exported intercept (6.3136) already includes it. README line 187 says 'The intercept was then multiplied by 1.00075'. Taken literally against the exported log-scale value, that is wrong: multiplying it would add about 0.0047 again. The README never asks a builder to apply the factor, so the risk is small. Low.

finding: OTHER is the base level of three crosses and pools mixed rare cells. Cells under 0.5% of exposure merge into OTHER. Because levels sort by code point, OTHER is the base level (coefficient 0) of the elevation*flood_zone, elevation*x_fz3_rain and prior_claims_5y*x_clay_dry crosses, so those relativities are relative to a mixed pool. For quotes, every combination of non-missing bands occurs in 2025, so an unseen cell arises only from a missing value (S5).
evidence: Mappings and row file. Merged into OTHER: distance*flood 8 cells (2.44% of exposure), elevation*flood 5 (1.47%), elevation*x_fz3_rain 1 (0.45%), prior*clay 1 (0.34%). OTHER rows in sample: distance*flood MSLE 0.0135 against 0.0082 for the rest; elevation*flood total +1.0%; prior*clay -1.9%. Suggested fix: Set a populous cell as the base and say what OTHER holds; or, with tree-threshold bands, merge the rare cells into a neighbour rather than into a pool.
verifier: Low; one supporting claim is wrong. Levels sort by code point, so OTHER is the base level of elevation*flood_zone, elevation*x_fz3_rain and prior_claims_5y*x_clay_dry; distance*flood's base is MISSING|q00. Cells merged into OTHER, with exposure share: distance*flood 8 cells (2.44%), elevation*flood 5 (1.47%), elevation*x_fz3_rain 1 (0.45%), prior*clay 1 (0.34%). OTHER rows: distance*flood MSLE 0.0134 against 0.0082; elevation*flood total +1.0%; prior*clay -1.9%. Predictions are unaffected; only how the cross tables read changes. The finding's claim that every non-missing band combination occurs in 2025 is false: distance q04 (>5.02 km) with flood q02 (zone 3 or above) is absent from the mappings, so a quote in that cell falls to OTHER with no missing value.

finding: what the reviewer checked
evidence:

Tests: 3 passed; test_export_excel plus test_surrogate_buildings, 15 passed from the scratch copy. The one failure in test_glm_lines in the scratch copy came from config.json not being copied there and is not a finding. ruff check --no-cache on the three changed Python files: all passed.

finding: run() has no tests, so intercept scaling, the SEEN branch, settle and the reconciliation logic are unprotected. tests/test_surrogate_buildings.py never calls run() or settle(). A regression in the intercept scaling, the SEEN lookup branch, the specification choice, checks_failed or the fitted_on wording passes every unit test. Some of these would surface only as 'checks failed' in a real run. M25 and M26 would put competition values into the committed terms.csv if the SEEN branch were ever taken, and M18 would silently pick the worst specification. Nothing catches any of those three.
evidence: Mutation run on a scratch copy of python/ and tests/ (the repository file was never imported; checked with sb.__file__, and cmp confirmed the scratch target was restored after each mutant). Command: .venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q -x tests/test_surrogate_buildings.py, once per mutant. The repository tests kill 13 of 31 mutants. Low, not medium. `grep settle|.run(` finds neither call in tests/test_surrogate_buildings.py, so every mutant inside run() or settle() survives. That branch copies export_excel.py lines 621-630, whose replacement step is also untested. No other runner in tests/ has a run()-level test either. finding: Unlisted interaction pair: the terms row says base level, the GLM and README say OTHER, and evaluate_glm raises. For an interaction pair with no row in the input mappings, the GLM's factors() maps it to OTHER, and the README says the same ('A pair not listed there is OTHER'). The exported '(any other level)' row (contribution 0.0, note 'scores as the base level') contradicts this whenever OTHER is a fitted level other than the base. In this export that is distance_to_river_km*flood_zone, whose OTHER coefficient is 0.0241. Its one possible but unlisted pair would be priced about 2.4% differently depending on which instruction the spreadsheet follows. evaluate_glm raises ValueError on any unlisted value, so the documented OTHER rule is never exercised. This has no effect on the 2025 book: every 2025 pair is listed and the reconciliation passes.
evidence: Possible pairs (interaction bands of a x b, MISSING included) were compared with the pairs listed in buildings_surrogate_input_mappings.csv. distance_to_river_km*flood_zone: 24 possible, 23 listed, 1 unlisted; OTHER coef 0.024079662602481892; base MISSING|q00. For elevation_m*flood_zone, elevation_m*x_fz3_rain and prior_claims_5y*x_clay_dry, OTHER is the base level (coefficient 0). The others have no OTHER level, so for them the two rules agree. A scratch probe on the synthetic surrogate set u*v to an unseen pair: glm.predict(unseen)/glm.predict(at OTHER) = 1.0 and /glm.predict(at base) = 1.3806; ex.evaluate_glm raised 'ValueError: u*v: values with no entry in the level map'; the '(any other level)' row read contribution [0.0] with the note 'scores as the base level'. Suggested fix: In export_glm, when 'OTHER' is in glm.levels[f], write the '(any other level)' row as 'maps to OTHER' with OTHER's contribution, or drop the row for such terms. Optionally give evaluate_glm a mode that maps unlisted values to OTHER, as factors() does, and add a unit test with an unseen crossing.
verifier: The numbers check out, but the claimed contradiction does not hold under the documented procedure. Recomputed from the committed files: distance_to_river_km*flood_zone has 24 possible pairs and 23 listed. The unlisted pair is q04|q02, a combination absent from the 2025 book. finding: The aliasing disclosure blames the crosses, but two-thirds of the rank deficit is between two main terms (renewal count and customer-since year). The README (line 224) and A35 (AUDIT_LOG.md line 933) explain the rank deficit (516 columns, rank 487) as main terms and crosses overlapping, and tell the reader to read only interacted features by their effect on price. In fact 19 of the 29 missing dimensions are already in the main-effects design, 17 of them because renewal_count and customer_since_year are one-to-one in 2025. Both are non-interacted features, and each one's rows carry only a share of a single shared effect.
evidence: Scratch refit of the final spec with fit_surrogate(x, y, ..., 12, 2.0) reproduced rows_surrogate_buildings.parquet exactly (max relative difference 0.0). models.design_matrix with an intercept column gave 516 columns and np.linalg.matrix_rank 487 (agrees with the reconciliation). Main-term columns only: 398 columns, rank 379, so 19 short. Dropping renewal_count leaves 381 columns at rank 379 (2 short), and dropping customer_since_year as well leaves 364 at rank 363. The 118 cross columns add only 108 to the rank, so the crosses account for 10. pd.crosstab(renewal_count, customer_since_year) on the 2025 rows shows exactly one customer-since year for each of the 18 renewal counts. In buildings_surrogate_terms.csv the coefficients mirror each other: renewal_count q16 = customer_since_year q01 = -0.00797224413957243, renewal q15 = customer q02 = -0.0011968, renewal q13 = customer q04 = -0.00045368. Suggested fix: State that renewal count and customer-since year are aliased in 2025 (customer-since year equals 2025 minus renewal count): add their two rows together and do not read either one alone. Attribute the deficit correctly (about 19 of 29 among main terms, 10 from crosses). Add that outside 2025, where the pairing shifts by a year, the split between them is not identified. The effects are small (log contributions of 0.015 or less).
verifier: Reproduced. I refitted fit_surrogate(x, y, ..., 12, 2.0) in scratch and applied the intercept factor. It matches rows_surrogate_buildings.parquet with a max relative difference of 0.0. Design matrix plus intercept: 516 columns, rank 487. Main terms only: 398 columns, rank 379, so 19 short. Without renewal_count: 381 columns, rank 379. Without customer_since_year as well: 364 columns, rank 363. The 118 cross columns add 108 to the rank, so the crosses account for 10 of the 29. pd.crosstab shows exactly one customer_since_year per renewal_count, and customer_since_year + renewal_count == 2025 on 100% of rows. In terms.csv the coefficients mirror each other, e.g. renewal q16 = customer q01 = -0.00797224413957243. finding: 'Four highest-gain split points' includes near-duplicate and empty cuts, so the crosses are coarser than the wording suggests. The description is literally true, but the top-4-by-gain rule picks clustered thresholds. Several bands are slivers or empty, and most exposure sits in one band, so each cross resolves about one boundary per feature.
evidence: Independent recomputation from buildings_xgboost.json matches the exported band edges. The selected cuts are: year built 1943, 1944, 1945, 1953; sum insured 105k, 182k, 207k, 209k; x_clay_dry 0.585, 0.696, 0.699, 0.789; distance 0.47, 0.50, 0.78, 0.85; elevation 2.1, 2.2, 2.5, 2.8; x_fz3_rain 0.624, 0.656, 0.714, 0.784; flood zone 3, 4, 5, 10.00001. Exposure shares from the exported bands: year built 1943 0.72% and 1944 0.80%; sum insured 207-209k 0.98%; x_clay_dry 0.696-0.699 0.20%; distance 0.47-0.50 0.63%; x_fz3_rain bands q01-q03 0.00%, 0.00%, 0.02% (so in effect zero against non-zero); flood zone q04 (above 10.00001) holds no row. Top bands: elevation above 2.8 m 81.6%, sum insured above 209k 63.2%, year built after 1953 61.1%, distance above 0.85 km 70.2%. This does follow the trees' gain: year built 1943-45 carry 69% of that feature's split gain, and the 10.00001 flood-zone cut carries 0.2%. The rule is not wrong; the wording overstates the resolution. Suggested fix: Disclose that the cuts cluster (with the top-band shares), or merge thresholds within a tolerance before taking the top four so that each feature gets distinct boundaries.
